text:
The commander's face fills the display. It is a face you know well. They speak in your voice, a half-second ahead of your thoughts.

"We found them."

$PersonRank $personName looks vaguely displeased.

"If we find you running with the transponder off again, you won't get off so easily."

The comm link is cut before you have a chance to respond.

$PersonRank $personName looks vaguely displeased.

"If we find you running with the transponder on again, you won't get off so easily."

The comm link is cut before you have a chance to respond.

The Afterlight drifts here with its running lights lit, hull unmarked. Every instrument you have says the ship is whole and empty.

The glow from its forward ports is a violet that does not match the light of the star, and it is turned toward you. Something in you wants very much to look at it directly.
options:

vd3NoLook:Don't look at the light

text:
The Afterlight is here again.

It was not here when the battle began. Your sensor logs say so, and they also say it has always been exactly here. Its running lights are lit, its hull unmarked, and the violet glow from its forward ports is steady and patient, like something that has been waiting for you to finish.

text:
A wreck drifts here, stripped to the frame. Its transponder is dead, but the hull is yours: the same lines, the same scoring along the port side, the same repairs in the same places.

The name on the bow reads $global.afl_copyName.

Nothing aboard is powered, but the data core is warm.

The log is intact, and it is yours. It lists the last jumps in order: $global.afl_logList. Each entry has the time of arrival, the fuel burned and the officer on watch. The officer on watch is always you.

The last entry begins: "Arrived at $global.afl_logLast. Quiet. I keep thinking the ship behind us is not behind us at all, that it is where we are going, that it is already there, it is--"

It stops there. Not cut off. Stopped, the way a sentence stops when the person writing it is called away.

The cargo holds are sealed, but the seals are your seals, and they open to your codes. Inside, the crates are stacked the way you would have stacked them, strapped down with the knots your crew favors. The labels are in your quartermaster's handwriting.

There is a great deal here. You are not sure whose it was.
The holds are bare. There is nothing left here that you would not rather have on your own ship.
options: vd8Shuttle:Order a shuttle to transfer the cargo to your ship

text:
The hold you are standing in has the same grey deck plates as your own. The same patched bulkhead, the same dent by the hatch. The scuffs under your boots are the ones you know.

You are on your own ship. You are also certain you walked here from the wreck.

A crew member's voice comes over the channel, patient and ordinary.

"Orders, Captain?"
